title: Legacy CRM Technical Architecture — Managed Package Namespace and Metadata Taxonomy
summary: The managed package namespace architecture and metadata taxonomy for a legacy life sciences CRM, covering eight distinct package namespaces, their metadata object distributions (custom objects, custom metadata types, custom settings, platform events, record types), and the trigger/validation rule layers that enforce business logic across packages.

findings.package_namespace_inventory: Eight managed package namespaces organize the platform metadata. The primary namespace contains the core CRM objects and the majority of triggers (approximately 230 pages of trigger documentation spanning pages 69-298). Extension namespaces add domain-specific capabilities: one for advanced engagement features (triggers on pages 299-321), one for compliance and regulatory functions (triggers on pages 322-324), one for content management, one for meetings and events (triggers on pages 325-335), one for remote engagement and digital channels (triggers on pages 336-414), one for provider data integration, and one for engagement messaging. Each namespace maintains independent versioning and upgrade paths while sharing a common data model through cross-namespace object references.
findings.metadata_object_distribution: Each package namespace contains five categories of metadata: (1) Standard objects extended with custom fields — accounts, contacts, and other platform objects augmented with life sciences-specific fields. (2) Custom objects — the bulk of the data model, with the primary namespace containing 200+ custom objects across functional domains. (3) Custom metadata types — configuration records that define platform behavior without requiring code changes (feature flags, navigation icons, formula configurations, integration mappings). (4) Custom settings — hierarchical and list-type settings for org-level, profile-level, and user-level configuration overrides. (5) Platform events — event-driven messaging objects used for real-time notifications, synchronization signals, and cross-system integration triggers.
findings.trigger_architecture: The trigger layer spans all eight namespaces with the primary namespace containing the vast majority of trigger logic. Triggers are organized by functional domain rather than by object — a single object may have triggers from multiple domains (e.g., the Account object has triggers from account management, territory management, and compliance domains). The trigger framework uses a handler pattern where trigger files delegate to handler classes, enabling selective activation/deactivation of business logic through configuration. The primary namespace alone contains approximately 230 pages of trigger documentation, indicating hundreds of individual trigger definitions.
findings.validation_rule_coverage: Validation rules span five namespaces: the primary namespace (pages 417-503, approximately 86 pages), the engagement extension (pages 504-516), the content namespace (page 517), the remote engagement namespace (pages 518-523), and the provider data integration namespace (pages 524-525). Additionally, workflow rules exist for the provider data integration namespace (page 526). The validation rule layer enforces data integrity constraints that complement the trigger-based business logic, ensuring that records meet minimum quality standards before trigger processing begins.

title: Legacy CRM Technical Architecture — CRM DataModel Domain Map and Object Distribution
summary: The complete CRM data model domain map for a legacy life sciences CRM, documenting 30+ functional domains with their object counts, page spans, and inter-domain relationships across account management, business planning, execution, integration, platform infrastructure, and samples management.

findings.account_management_cluster: Six sub-domains centered on healthcare provider and organization management: Account Management (page 527, 20+ objects covering accounts, addresses, affiliations, relationships, account hierarchy), Account Merge Management (page 719, duplicate resolution and merge tracking), Activity History (page 726, historical interaction aggregation), ADA Lite (page 734, next best customer recommendation engine), BestTime (page 739, provider visit timing optimization), and ClinicalTrial (page 747, 8 objects for trial site and investigator tracking). Supporting sub-domains include Data Change Request (page 781, 7 objects for field-initiated data correction workflows), HCO/HCP Dashboard (page 797, organization and provider summary visualization), Ratings (page 940, 9 objects for provider profiling scores and segmentation), and Search Before Create (page 962, duplicate detection during account creation).
findings.business_planning_cluster: Five sub-domains for cyclical planning and territory operations: Account Plan (page 1047, 15+ objects for strategic account planning with objectives, tactics, and stakeholder mapping), Activity Plan (page 1157, cyclical visit planning with target frequencies and product priorities), Calendar (page 1187, scheduling and availability management), Call Plan (page 1206, visit sequence optimization), and Plan Cycle (page 1221, temporal planning periods that govern all business planning activities). The Admin sub-domain (page 970) covers User management, Product Admin (page 990, 9+ objects for product hierarchy and therapeutic area classification), Territory Admin (page 1025, geographic and organizational territory definition), TimeOfTerritory (page 1039, representative-to-territory temporal assignments), and Mobile (page 988, mobile device management). A version comparison section (pages 1241-1273) documents the v19 to v20 evolution, tracking every object and field added, modified, or deprecated between major releases.
findings.execution_cluster: Twelve sub-domains covering field force execution: Call (page 1343, 20+ objects for visit recording, attendee tracking, product discussion capture, key message delivery), Compliance (page 1497, 7 objects for regulatory tracking and HCP interaction limits), eDetailing/CLM (page 1532, 15+ objects for closed-loop marketing with slide-level analytics), Email (page 1581, template-driven compliant email with tracking), Inquiries 2.0 (page 1619, medical information request management), Insight (page 1631, field intelligence and recommendation delivery), Medical Inquiry Request (page 1647, detailed clinical question routing), Order2 (page 1668, order management with pricing objects covering price books, tiered pricing rules, and approval workflows), Remote Engagement (page 1740, digital detailing sessions), Remote Session (page 1745, video conferencing integration), and OCE Connect (page 1666, cross-system connectivity). MeetingsEvents Management (page 1751, 25+ objects for speaker programs, educational events, attendee management, logistics, and budgets) and Meetings FMV (page 1971, Fair Market Value tracking with Agreement, Invoice, and logistics objects) form a dedicated events sub-cluster.
findings.integration_and_platform_cluster: Integration domains include: ApprovalInquiry (page 2356, approval workflow integration), Concur (page 2363, expense management connector), CrossOrg (page 2364, multi-org data sharing), MCM (page 2368, multi-channel messaging), and WeChat (page 2398, messaging platform integration). Platform domains include: App Store (page 2406, application catalog), Audit Handler (page 2409, audit trail infrastructure), DynamicTreeView (page 2411, hierarchical data visualization), Error Logging (page 2416, centralized error capture), Feature Activation (page 2424, feature flag management), Generic Workflow (page 2428, 15+ objects for configurable workflow engine), iOS Support Offline/Online (page 2469, synchronization infrastructure with objects governing what data syncs to mobile devices and in what order), Metadata Store (page 2521, metadata versioning and caching), Notification (page 2537, push and in-app notification delivery), Reporting (page 2545), ScheduledJob (page 2546, background job orchestration), Timeline (page 2552, chronological activity visualization), UI and Configuration Layer (page 2554, 25+ objects for the metadata-driven Dynamic UI renderer), UnitTest (page 2599, test infrastructure), and UserFeedback (page 2600, in-app feedback capture).
findings.samples_and_connectors: Samples Limit (page 2603, regulatory quantity limits for sample disbursement), Samples Management (page 2615, the complete compliant sample distribution lifecycle — inventory, disbursement, signature capture, lot tracking, and regulatory reporting), SFDC Connector (page 2687, platform-to-platform data synchronization), SFDC Concur Connector (page 2690, expense report integration), SFDC Organization Manager Connector (page 2695, organizational hierarchy synchronization), Opt Management (page 2212, communication preference and consent tracking), Pharmacy Orders (page 2222, pharmacy-specific ordering workflows), Projections (page 2293, sales forecast and target tracking), StoreManagement (page 2312, retail point-of-sale integration), and Survey (page 2343, in-field survey creation and response collection).

title: Legacy CRM Technical Architecture — Engagement Platform and Third-Party Connector Objects
summary: The engagement platform and third-party integration architecture for a legacy life sciences CRM, covering digital messaging objects, remote engagement infrastructure, provider data connectors, expense management integration, and the version evolution model that tracks cross-release compatibility.

findings.engage_messaging_objects: The Engage namespace (Engage DM, page 1274) contains 30+ objects dedicated to compliant digital messaging between field representatives and healthcare providers. The object model covers: message templates with approval workflow tracking, message delivery status and tracking (sent, delivered, read, bounced), consent management for digital communication channels, content fragment libraries for reusable message components, recipient list management with segmentation capabilities, campaign orchestration linking messages to marketing initiatives, and analytics objects capturing engagement metrics (open rates, click-through, response times). The Engage platform operates under strict compliance constraints — every message must use an approved template, and all interactions are logged for regulatory audit.
findings.remote_engagement_infrastructure: Remote engagement spans two sub-domains: Remote Engagement (page 1740) for asynchronous digital detailing and Remote Session (page 1745) for synchronous video conferencing. The remote session infrastructure includes: session scheduling and invitation objects, participant management with role differentiation (presenter, attendee, moderator), content sharing state tracking (which presentation is active, which slide is displayed), screen annotation and collaboration objects, session recording consent and storage references, and post-session analytics (attendance duration, content engagement, participant interaction counts). This infrastructure supports both one-to-one provider meetings and one-to-many educational events conducted remotely.
findings.provider_data_and_expense_connectors: Third-party integration connectors include: (1) Provider data integration (QIDC namespace) — connects to external healthcare provider and organization databases for master data enrichment, including objects for data matching rules, match confidence scoring, data stewardship workflows, and synchronization status tracking. Workflow rules (page 526) automate provider data update approvals. (2) Concur expense management connector (page 2363, plus SFDC Concur Connector page 2690) — integrates expense reporting with CRM activities, linking expense line items to specific field visits, meetings, or events for compliance tracking. (3) WeChat integration (page 2398) — messaging platform connector for markets where WeChat is the primary digital communication channel, with objects for official account binding, template message management, and interaction tracking. (4) MCM multi-channel messaging (page 2368) — orchestration layer that routes messages across email, digital messaging, and third-party channels based on provider communication preferences.
findings.version_evolution_model: The v19 to v20 comparison section (pages 1241-1273, approximately 32 pages) documents the formal version evolution model. Each major release tracks: objects added (new functional capabilities), objects modified (field additions, field type changes, field deprecation), objects deprecated (marked for removal in future releases), and behavioral changes (trigger logic modifications, validation rule updates). This version comparison documentation enables customers to assess upgrade impact on their customizations, integrations, and data migration requirements. The evolution model demonstrates that each major release adds approximately 20-40 new objects while modifying 50-100 existing objects, reflecting continuous functional expansion while maintaining backward compatibility.

title: Legacy CRM Technical Architecture — Platform Infrastructure Objects and iOS Offline Architecture
summary: The platform infrastructure layer and iOS offline synchronization architecture for a legacy life sciences CRM, covering the sync engine object model, metadata-driven UI configuration layer, feature activation framework, generic workflow engine, error logging infrastructure, and scheduled job orchestration.

findings.ios_offline_sync_architecture: The iOS Support Offline/Online domain (page 2469) contains the synchronization infrastructure that governs data movement between the server and mobile devices. Key architectural components include: sync definition objects that declare which objects sync to mobile and in what priority order, sync filter objects that limit which records sync based on territory assignment, ownership, and recency criteria, sync status tracking objects that record per-device sync progress (last sync timestamp, records synced, errors encountered), conflict resolution objects that define how server-client data conflicts are resolved (server wins, client wins, or manual resolution based on object type), and delta sync objects that track incremental changes since the last successful sync to minimize data transfer. The sync architecture must balance completeness (representatives need all relevant data offline) against performance (syncing too much data degrades device performance and battery life).
findings.ui_configuration_layer: The UI and Configuration Layer (page 2554) contains 25+ objects that power the metadata-driven Dynamic UI renderer. This layer includes: page layout definition objects that map field arrangements to record types and profiles, section configuration objects that define collapsible sections with conditional visibility rules, related list configuration objects that control which child records appear and in what order, action configuration objects that define available buttons and their visibility conditions, quick action objects that provide streamlined record creation and update forms, and mobile-specific layout objects that adapt desktop layouts for tablet and phone form factors. The configuration layer also includes custom label objects for internationalization and menu tab objects for navigation structure definition.
findings.feature_activation_framework: Feature Activation (page 2424) provides a runtime feature flag system that controls which capabilities are available in each deployment. The framework includes: feature definition objects with activation status (active, inactive, beta), feature dependency objects that enforce prerequisite relationships between features (activating feature B requires feature A to be active), feature scope objects that control activation granularity (org-wide, profile-specific, user-specific), and feature audit objects that track activation/deactivation events with timestamps and responsible administrators. This framework enables gradual feature rollout, A/B testing of new capabilities, and customer-specific feature configurations without code deployment.
findings.generic_workflow_and_infrastructure: The Generic Workflow engine (page 2428, 15+ objects) provides a configurable workflow system separate from the platform's native workflow rules. Objects include: workflow definition (multi-step process templates with branching logic), workflow instance (running process instances with current step tracking), workflow step (individual steps with entry criteria, actions, and exit criteria), workflow assignment (step-to-user or step-to-queue routing rules), workflow history (complete audit trail of step transitions with timestamps and actors), and workflow notification (email and in-app alerts triggered by step transitions). Supporting infrastructure domains include: Error Logging (page 2416, centralized error capture with severity classification and stack trace storage), ScheduledJob (page 2546, background job orchestration for batch processing, data cleanup, and scheduled reports), Metadata Store (page 2521, metadata versioning and caching to reduce API calls and improve mobile performance), Notification (page 2537, unified push notification and in-app alert delivery), Timeline (page 2552, chronological activity visualization aggregating calls, emails, meetings, and other interactions into a single provider view), and Audit Handler (page 2409, compliance audit trail infrastructure separate from the platform's field history tracking).
